title: Cap. X: non-election / negative reprobation defined — not pre-damnation from foreseen final unbelief, but denial from mere will of the special mercy that softens and leads to life (Bradwardine; Rom. ix. 16, 18)
pass_a_gloss: So we say that Non-election, preterition or negative reprobation is by no means the pre-damnation of singular persons from their foreseen final unbelief and impenitence, (although we acknowledge such a decree) but from the mere will of God the denial of that special mercy which takes away unbelief and impenitence by softening, and leads unto everlasting life by establishing and conserving in faith and holiness. Or more briefly from our Bradwardine, who merited unto himself the surname of the profound Doctor, Predestination is the everlasting preparation by the Divine will of final grace in the way, and of everlasting beatitude in the fatherland, for certain rational creatures, lib. 1. cap. 45. pag. 421. And reprobation is the everlasting nilling of God of conferring such things in certain persons, Ibid. pag. 426. With the Apostle we defend that this election is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, but of God that shows mercy, Rom. ix. 16. and that this non-election, reprobation or everlasting nilling did not arise from foreseen unbelief, or impenitence of men, but from his mere liberty, who has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens, Rom. ix. 18. Which, Augustine interpreting, is as if the Apostle had said, on whom he wills he has mercy, and on whom he wills not he has not mercy, De praedest. et grat. cap. 6.
pass_b_english: So we put it this way. Non-election — preterition, negative reprobation — is not pre-damnation of singular persons from foreseen final unbelief and impenitence. (We do acknowledge a decree of that kind.) What it is, from God's mere will, is denial of that special mercy which softens away unbelief and impenitence, and which leads to everlasting life by fixing and keeping a person in faith and holiness. Bradwardine, our profound Doctor, says it shorter: Predestination is the eternal preparation by divine will of final grace in the way, and of eternal beatitude in the fatherland, for certain rational creatures (lib. 1. cap. 45. pag. 421). Reprobation is God's eternal nilling to confer such things in certain persons (Ibid. pag. 426). With the Apostle we hold that this election is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. ix. 16). And this non-election — this reprobation or eternal nilling — did not spring from men's foreseen unbelief or impenitence. It sprang from his mere liberty: who has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens (Rom. ix. 18). Augustine's reading is as if the Apostle had said: on whom he wills he has mercy, and on whom he wills not he has not mercy (De praedest. et grat. cap. 6).
source_text: Ita dicimus, Non-electionem, praeteritionem sive reprobationem negativam haud esse singularium personarum ex praevisa finali earundem infidelitate et impoenitentia praedamnationem, (quamvis tale decretum agnoscamus) sed ex mera Dei voluntate denegationem ejus specialis misericordiae, quae infidelitatem et impoenitentiam tollit emolliendo, et ad vitam aeternam perducit in fide et sanctitate stabiliendo et conservando. Vel brevius ex Bradwardino nostro, qui profundi Doctoris cognomentum sibi meruit, Praedestinatio est aeterna praeparatio a voluntate Divina gratiae finalis in via, et beatitudinis aeternae in patria, creaturis quibusdam rationalibus, lib. 1. cap. 45. pag. 421. Et reprobatio est aeterna Dei nolitio conferendi talia in quibusdam personis, Ibid. pag. 426. Cum Apostolo defendimus hanc electionem non esse volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei, Rom. ix. 16. et hanc non-electionem, reprobationem sive nolitionem aeternam non esse ortam ex praevisa infidelitate, aut impoenitentia hominum, sed ex mera ejus libertate, qui cujus vult miseretur, et quem vult indurat, Rom. ix. 18. Quod, interprete Augustino, perinde est ac si dixisset Apostolus, cujus vult miseretur, et cujus non vult non miseretur, De praedest. et grat. cap. 6.
